name: Amira Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights in Eastgate, the old east side of the city, mostly in a patrol car with another constable called Dev. We start at ten with a briefing, then it's calls: domestics, shop alarms, somebody shouting outside the kebab place on Mill Road at two in the morning. I'm still on probation, second year, so my sergeant reads everything I write.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people, honestly, even the hard ones. Sitting with an old man whose flat got broken into and making him a tea is the bit that feels like the job. What wears me out is the tablet. Every call means twenty minutes of boxes on the report system, and I'm slow at it, so I end up staying an hour past shift to finish. That's unpaid, by the way.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Joel in a rented flat above a laundrette on Canal Street. He's a care home aide, so between the two of us we're both on lower pay and odd hours. We've got maybe two weeks of rent put by, and the landlord just put the rent up eight percent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Honestly, part of me would be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that the job is about people and no computer was going to change that. At the station I'd probably joke that the tablet is still the worst thing that ever happened to policing. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the officers' association about funding being the real problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, nothing changes for me, and nothing changing isn't great either. The council has already cut overtime, and overtime is what kept Joel and me from going into the red last winter. I'm still on probation, and if my reports stay slow, that goes in my review. So I'd still be lying awake about money, just not about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and try to get faster on the report system, maybe ask Dev to sit with me for a couple of hours. We'd cut the takeaway on Friday nights and I'd stop driving to work, take the night bus instead. And I'd go to the next association meeting about overtime, because that's where the money actually is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Not scared. It's the same worry I've had since I joined, just without a new one added on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take the night bus. What does that save, and what does it cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It saves maybe forty a month in fuel and parking. The cost is the walk from the bus stop at seven in the morning, which is fine, I'm police. But I'd be lying if I said it doesn't feel a bit silly, a constable who can't afford to drive to my own station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the overtime doesn't come back, which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract, probably, or we'd pay the electric late. Rent always goes first because the landlord is looking for an excuse. Joel's already asked about extra shifts at the care home, but they cut his hours too.

say: The job is about **people**, and no computer was ever going to change that.
The real problem in policing is **funding and overtime**, not technology.
think: Nothing changing still leaves me **short every month** on rent and bills.
My **slow reports** could hurt my probation review even without any new AI.
do: Ask Dev for **two hours of help** on the report system this month.
Take the **night bus** instead of driving to save about forty a month.
Go to the next **association meeting** about overtime cuts.
feel: **Tired** rather than scared, carrying the same money worry as before.
S0.quote: I'd be lying if I said it doesn't feel a bit silly, a constable who can't afford to drive to my own station.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **money and probation**, not technology, and it was there before AI came up.
She treats the **report tablet** as the enemy; slow typing costs her unpaid hours.
Blames **council cuts** for overtime loss and looks to the officers' association to fix it.

steps.text: Keep working Eastgate night shifts and practise reports with Dev
Take the night bus instead of driving to save fuel
Attend the officers' association meeting about overtime cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like what they're already trying. Last spring they piloted a thing that writes the report from the body camera.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the same as the association: fine, use it for paperwork, but don't use it as an excuse to hire fewer officers. Online I'd share posts about keeping humans on the phones, because people calling about a domestic need a real person. I'd sign the petition, put my name on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I'm the officer they'd be glad to swap for software. I'm slow on the tablet and I don't use any of that AI stuff, and Sergeant Okafor already says my reports read like I wrote them in a moving car. If the system writes reports, the officers who can check it fast look good, and I'm not one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on patrol, because that's the hands-on part and it's the part they still need. I'd ask the association to fight for training in work time, because I'm not paying for a course out of what we've got. We'd also stop the gym membership and I'd sell my old bike to put a couple of hundred aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's moving and I'm the last one to notice. I don't want to learn a new system every year. I joined to be out on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. If the force made the report tool compulsory, what would you do on your first shift with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably ask Dev to show me and then do it the long way anyway, writing in my notebook first. I know that sounds stubborn. I just don't trust a camera to understand what a frightened woman meant when she said she was fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the station would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The call handlers in the control room, more than us. They're mostly women on low pay, and answering calls is exactly what the card says goes first. My friend Priya works there and she's already been told the overnight team is being reviewed.

say: Use AI for **paperwork**, but never as an excuse to hire **fewer officers**.
People calling about a domestic need a **real person** on the phone, not software.
think: I'm the **slow officer** on the tablet, so I'd look worst next to the software.
Patrol is the **hands-on part**, and that's where I'm safest for now.
do: Push the association to win **paid training** during shift time.
Cancel the **gym membership** and sell the old bike for about two hundred.
Stay on **street patrol** and avoid desk roles.
feel: Left behind, like the **ground is moving** and nobody told her.
**Stubborn** pride about being a street officer.
S1.quote: I just don't trust a camera to understand what a frightened woman meant when she said she was fine.
fieldNote: She sees her **probation review** at risk because the thinking work is exactly where she's weakest.
Her concern quickly turns to the **control room staff**, mostly low-paid women.
Resists the tool but would still **go through the motions**; the gap is between compliance and trust.

steps.text: Stay on Eastgate street patrol and turn down desk postings
Ask the association to win paid training on shift
Cancel the gym and sell the old bike for savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the fast ones. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be twenty-nine. That's before I've even finished being new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need public control of this stuff, not companies selling it to police forces. At the station I'd say I'm not handing my radio to a robot, and people would laugh. Online I'd probably post something angry and then delete it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the force would shrink fast. If AI does every report, every call log, every bit of planning by 2028, then they only need officers for the hands-on stuff, and three years later robots do some of that too. Last in, first out. I'm last in. Joel's job is hands-on as well, but care homes will want robots as soon as they're cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd go to the association and ask what protection probationers get, in writing. I'd pick up every overtime shift going while it lasts and put it straight into savings, even fifty a week. And I'd ask my mum if we could move into her spare room if it came to it, which I really don't want to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I'd be lying in bed working out how many months we'd last, and the answer is about one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters, but not enough. The reports and the calls go in 2028, and that's half my shift. The walking around, the knocking on doors, the holding someone's arm, that goes around 2031. So I'd get three years of being a constable who only does the physical bits, probably on worse pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Joel the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're not panicking, and then I'd panic in the bathroom. He'd say his residents won't want a robot washing them, and I'd want to believe him. We'd sit down with the bank app that night, I know that much.

say: This is why **public control** of AI matters, not companies selling it to forces.
I'm **not handing my radio** to a robot, and I'd say so at the station.
think: The force would shrink fast, and as a probationer I'm **last in, first out**.
Joel's **care home job** looks hands-on, but cheap robots would reach it too.
do: Ask the association for **written protection** for probationers straight away.
Take every **overtime shift** and save at least fifty a week.
Ask her mum about **moving into** the spare room if needed.
feel: **Sick** with worry, counting about **one month** of savings.
S2.quote: The reports and the calls go in 2028, and that's half my shift.
fieldNote: She understands the **three-year gap** but sees only a smaller, worse-paid job in it.
Both household jobs feel **exposed**; she expects to lose hers as a probationer.
Public anger, private planning around her **mum's spare room**; she hates the fallback.

steps.text: Ask the officers' association for written job protection for probationers
Take every overtime shift and save fifty a week
Ask her mum about moving into the spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, more time. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be thirty-two. That's a bit better, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things, maybe louder, because with five years there's time to actually organise. I'd be at the association meetings and probably at a march outside city hall. Online I'd share stuff about a guarantee for public sector jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd get through probation and maybe a couple of years as a proper constable. But I'm not the kind to turn myself into a tech person. Watching it come slowly might be worse than it hitting me all at once, because I'm not the kind to turn myself into a tech person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save a proper cushion, three months, which for us means cutting everything we can and taking the extra shifts. I'd look at the jobs that stay hands-on longest, maybe custody or prisoner transport, and ask about a transfer. And I'd ask the association to push for retraining money from the council before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like a date on the calendar I keep looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not the kind to turn yourself into a tech person. If the force paid for a course, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they paid and it was in work time, yes, I'd go. I'd sit at the back and complain the whole time. But I wouldn't turn down free help, I'm not that stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would three months of savings actually take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three thousand, which is nearly a year of cutting back for us. No holiday, no takeaways, the car sold and the bus everywhere. Joel's sister's wedding is next year and we'd probably not go.

say: Five years is time to **organise**, so I'd be at meetings and marches.
Public sector workers need a **job guarantee** before this arrives.
think: I'd get through **probation**, but I won't turn into a **tech person**.
Watching it come slowly might be **worse** than a sudden hit.
do: Save toward **three thousand**, about three months of costs, by selling the car.
Ask about a **transfer to custody** or prisoner transport, which stays hands-on longer.
Push the association to win **retraining money** from the council.
feel: **Heavy**, like a date circled on the calendar.
S3.quote: Watching it come slowly might be worse than it hitting me all at once, because I'm not the kind to turn myself into a tech person.
fieldNote: Five years gives her time to **organise politically**, which suits her outlook.
Would take **free training** in work time despite resisting technology.
Her plan is to hide in the **most hands-on** corners of policing.

steps.text: Sell the car and save toward three thousand
Ask about a transfer to the custody suite
Push the association to secure council retraining money
March at city hall for a public sector job guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career stage away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say we've got time to get the rules right, and the unions should be at the table now. At work it would be a background thing, something people joke about in the canteen. Online I'd share the occasional article, nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels far enough that I'd push it to the back of my mind, which I know is a mistake. By 2036 I'd be a constable with ten years in and nothing else on my CV. If the force halves after that, I'd be thirty-seven with no other trade and few jobs like this around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd just keep going and try to build the cushion slowly. Maybe in a few years I'd look at something like a youth worker course, because that's people work and it's what I'm actually good at. And I'd keep paying into the pension, even when it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A low hum of worry. Not panic, just there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said pushing it to the back of your mind would be a mistake. What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone I know lose their job to it, honestly. If my friend Priya in the control room got let go, I'd stop pretending about AI. Until then it's a story on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still doing people work, even if it's not policing. Maybe still with Joel, in a flat we don't have to fight the landlord over. That's not much to ask, is it?

say: We have **time to set rules**, so unions should be at the table now.
It would stay a **canteen joke** at work for years.
think: Ten years is far enough that I'd **ignore it**, and I know that's a mistake.
At thirty-seven I'd have **no other trade** and few jobs like mine nearby.
do: Keep building a **small cushion** slowly from each pay packet.
Look at a **youth worker course** in a few years.
Keep paying into the **pension** even when money is tight.
feel: A **low hum** of worry, not panic.
S4.quote: If my friend Priya in the control room got let go, I'd stop pretending about AI.
fieldNote: The long warning makes her **put it off**, which she admits openly.
Her fallback idea, **youth work**, keeps her in people work rather than tech.
Still tight on money, so even the slow case leaves her **income exposed** later in her career.

steps.text: Keep working patrol shifts in Eastgate
Keep paying into the police pension each month
Look into a part-time youth worker course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. I'd be a probationer when it hits and that's the worst place to be. What would help is a promise from the council that nobody gets cut without retraining in work time, and someone to fight for us. Rent controls too, honestly, because our landlord is half the problem.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why I joined. I joined because a woman officer sat with my mum the night my dad left, and she was kind. No machine is going to be kind like that. If the bosses forget that, they've lost the point of the job.

headlineQuote: A woman officer sat with my mum the night my dad left, and she was kind. No machine is going to be kind like that.
portrait: A **27-year-old probationer** on night patrol in Eastgate, living with her partner Joel above a laundrette.
**Two weeks of rent** saved, a rising rent bill and cut overtime keep her anxious even with no AI change.
Avoids technology and is **slow on reports**, which she knows makes her look replaceable.
Leans on the **officers' association** and politics, blaming council cuts and companies selling AI to police.
Grows **alarmed** at the two-year case and puts off acting when there are ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she would still be a probationer and expects last in, first out.
whatWouldHelp: A council promise of **retraining in work time** before any cuts, with the union fighting for it.
**Rent controls**, since the landlord's increases squeeze her household already.
